files.description: Afrasiyab Killing Naudar (detail), a folio from the Great Mongol Shahnama (Book of Kings) "Several scenes show murders, beheadings and executions as well as a poisoning, a castration and a flaying, many of them examples of the public spectacles of pain designed to create a sense of legitimacy in this highly militarised period (Figure 28.8). Art here is propaganda in service to the Mongol court, and the pictures reflect the turbulent times in which this stunning manuscript was produced." Blair S. Picturing Violence in the Islamic Lands. In: Gordon MS, Kaeuper RW, Zurndorfer H, eds. The Cambridge World History of Violence. The Cambridge World History of Violence. Cambridge University Press; 2020:576-600, p.593

files.title: File:Bahram Gur in a peasant's house.jpg
files.description: Bahram Gur in a peasant's house, Folio from the Great Mongol Shahnama. 40 x 28.6 cm. Tabriz, c. 1335. McGill University Library Ms. Persian 6 "Although the initial use of images of royal power in manuscript illustration appears to have been as a frontispiece, they gradually influenced the representation of stories. An early example would appear to be the painting of Bahrim Gur in a peasant's house from the Demotte Shahnamah. Although the setting of the event was the home of a peasant, Bahram sits on a throne equipped with cushions situated in a tiled recess. Here the formal image of the ruler's throne has intruded on the subject represented" Comments on Persian Painting Priscilla Soucek Iranian Studies, Vol. 7, No. 1/2, Studies on Isfahan: Proceedings of the Isfahan Colloquium, Part I (Winter - Spring, 1974), pp. 72-87 (16 pages)

File:Iran, Tabriz, Mongol Period (Ilkhanid), 14th Century - Text Page, Persian Verses (Recto); The Fortieth Year of King Kisra Nushirwa - 1959.330.a - Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg
files.description: Mongol interest in the production of illustrated manuscripts evenutally focused on Persian epic poetry. The Shahnama, a compilation of the epics and tales of Iran's legendary heroes, was a natural choice; the book included many subjects that suited Mongol taste, such as banquets, battles, hunting, and magical or fantastic events. Seated on the throne in the center of the painting is the Sasanian ruler of Iran, Khusraw I Anushirwan (531–579), descendant of Bahram Gur (seen killing a dragon in CMA 1943.658). Above the king's head an inscription reads, "Picture of Nushirwan the Just." The figure in the elaborate turban to the left of the king is probably the young Minister Buzurgmihr, famous for his wisdom and virtue. To celebrate the explanation of a troublesome dream by Buzurgmihr, Nushirwan held a series of seven banquets. The text around this painting describes the fifth banquet.
files.usageterms: Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication

files.title: File:Iran, Tabriz, Ilkhanid period - Bahram Gur Arrives at the House of a Merchant, text page (recto); Bahram Gu - 1943.658 - Cleveland Museum of Art.tif
files.description: In this intense painting, Bahram Gur plunges his sword into the breast of a dragon. A favorite character from Iran's pre-Islamic history, Bahram Gur (reigned 420–38) was a popular ruler of the Sassanian dynasty and a great hunter. He took the name "Gur," meaning onager (a wild ass), because it was his preferred game, although he also excelled at killing dragons. As evidenced by this illustration's rock formations, tree trunk, and dragon, Iranian painting in the Mongol period borrowed numerous stylistic and spatial elements from Chinese models. With the surging landscape and writhing dragon rendered with equal energy, this is a picture of extraordinary unity and concentration.
files.usageterms: Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication

files.title: File:Jalayirid Shāhnāma court scene, Tabriz or Baghdad, ca. 1370–74. Bifolio, TSMK, H. 2153, fols. 55r, 54v.jpg
files.description: Jalayirid Shāhnāma court scene, Tabriz or Baghdad, ca. 1370–74. Bifolio, TSMK, H. 2153, fols. 55r, 54v Tabriz or Baghdad 1325-35. Scene from the Shahnamah "An extraordinarily detailed Ilkhanid princely interior is the setting for a subject rarely, if ever, illustrated in copies of the Shahnama: Kay Khusrau victorious over Ahriman and the divs at the castle of Bahman. Firdausi writes that Kay Khusrau then erected the fire-temple of Azargushasp beside the castle, returning there for ceremonial events several times during his long reign". A possible depiction of Abaqa Khan at the Il-Khanid court, in Takht-e Soleymān. pp. 188-189 (in English) (1 January 2002) Peerless Images: Persian Painting and Its Sources , Yale University Press, pp. 188−189 ISBN : 978-0-300-09038-3 .

files.title: File:Miniature from the love story of Zal and Rudaba, from a 14th-century manuscript of the Shahnama, known as the Great Ilkhanid Shahnama.jpg
files.description: A miniature from the story of Zal and Rudaba, one of the most important love stories in the Shahnama, from the Great Ilkhanid Shahnama. This manuscript was produced in the 1330s for Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, the last Chinggisid monarch of Iran. Today, only scattered folios survive in museums and private collections around the world.
